title: Information & Entropy
description: Measure information as surprise and find the average information a source produces.

study.title: Self-information
study.body: An outcome with probability $p$ carries $-\log_2 p$ bits of information: the rarer the event, the bigger the surprise when it happens. A fair coin flip gives 1 bit, one of 8 equally likely outcomes 3 bits, and a certain event 0 bits. For **independent** events the probabilities multiply, so their informations add.

study.title: Entropy of a source
study.body: A source emits symbols $x_i$ with probabilities $p_i$. Its **entropy** is the average information per symbol, the expected surprise. It is about the least average number of yes/no questions needed to identify a symbol and, as the source-coding unit shows, the fewest bits per symbol that any lossless code can reach. Symbols with $p_i = 0$ add nothing (take $0\log 0 = 0$).

study.title: Explore: the binary entropy function
study.body: A binary source sends a 1 with probability $p$ and a 0 with probability $1-p$. Its entropy $H(p)$ is 0 when the output is certain ($p$ = 0 or 1) and reaches its maximum of 1 bit at $p$ = 0.5. The curve is symmetric and steep near the ends: $p$ = 0.11 already gives 0.5 bit. Drag $p$ and compare the information of a 1 and of a 0 with their average.

study.title: Bounds on entropy
study.body: For a source with $M$ symbols the entropy lies between 0 and $\log_2 M$. It is 0 only when one symbol is certain, and it is $\log_2 M$ only when all $M$ symbols are **equally likely**: any imbalance makes the output more predictable. So a 12-bit ADC delivers at most 12 bits of information per sample, and only if all 4096 codes are equally likely.

study.title: Bits, nats and hartleys
study.body: The base of the logarithm only sets the unit: base 2 gives **bits**, base $e$ gives **nats** (common in derivations), base 10 gives **hartleys**. Convert like any logarithm: 1 nat = $\log_2 e$ = 1.443 bits and 1 hartley = $\log_2 10$ = 3.322 bits. Using $\log_{10}$ in a formula meant for bits is a classic mistake: it gives an answer 3.32 times too small.

study.title: Worked example: a four-symbol source
study.body:
A source sends A, B, C and D with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8, at 1000 symbols per second.
- Information per symbol: 1, 2, 3 and 3 bits.
- Entropy: $H$ = 0.5·1 + 0.25·2 + 0.125·3 + 0.125·3 = **1.75 bits/symbol**, less than the 2 bits of a fixed two-bit code.
- Information rate: $R = r_s H$ = 1000 × 1.75 = **1750 bit/s**.

study.title: Real sources: text and sensors
study.body: With 26 letters and a space, a uniform model gives $\log_2 27$ = 4.75 bits per character. Real letter frequencies (E is common, Z rare) bring this down to about 4.1 bits, and using the preceding letters as context lowers it much further: prediction experiments suggest roughly 1 to 1.5 bits per letter for English. Sensor data behave the same way: a slowly varying temperature read by a 12-bit ADC gives nearly the same code every sample, so the **differences** between samples have a small entropy, which is what compressors exploit.

steps.title: How much does an outcome tell you?
steps.body: Information measures surprise. Learning something that was certain tells you nothing; learning that a very unlikely event happened tells you a lot. Shannon's measure for an outcome with probability $p$ is $-\log_2 p$ bits: a fair coin gives 1 bit, one of four equally likely outcomes 2 bits.

steps.prompt: One of {{k||4}} equally likely messages is sent. How much information does receiving it give?
steps.explanation: Each message has $p$ = 1/{{k||4}}, so $I = -\log_2(1/{{k||4}}) = \log_2 {{k||4}}$ = **{{log2(k)}} bits**. Indeed, {{log2(k)}} yes/no questions, each halving the remaining possibilities, single out one of {{k||4}} messages.

steps.prompt: A fair {{N}}-sided die is rolled. How much information does the result give?
steps.explanation: Each face has $p$ = 1/{{N}}: $I = \log_2 {{N}}$ = **{{log2(N)}} bits**. {{log10(N)}} uses $\log_{10}$ (hartleys) and {{ln(N)}} uses $\ln$ (nats). {{ceil(log2(N))}} bits is what a fixed-length binary code needs per roll, which is more than the information.

steps.title: Information adds up
steps.body: For independent events the probabilities multiply, $p(x, y) = p(x)\,p(y)$, and the logarithm turns that product into a sum. Drawing a card from a deck tells you its suit ($\log_2 4$ = 2 bits) and its rank ($\log_2 13$ = 3.70 bits): together $\log_2 52$ = 5.70 bits.

steps.prompt: Each character of a password is chosen uniformly and independently from {{A}} possible symbols. How much information does a {{n}}-character password contain?
steps.explanation: Per character: $\log_2 {{A}}$ = {{log2(A)}} bits. Independent characters add: {{n}} × {{log2(A)}} = **{{n*log2(A)}} bits**, the same as $\log_2({{A}}^{ {{n}} })$ for the ${{A}}^{ {{n}} }$ equally likely passwords.

steps.prompt: A smoke detector reports an alarm with probability {{p}} per reading.

ask.prompt: How much information does an **alarm** reading carry?
ask.explanation: $I = -\log_2 p = -\log_2 {{p}}$ = **{{-log2(p)}} bits**. Rare events are very informative.

ask.prompt: How much information does a **normal** reading carry?
ask.explanation: $P(\text{normal}) = 1 - {{p}}$ = {{1-p||4}}, so $I = -\log_2({{1-p||4}})$ = **{{-log2(1-p)||3}} bits**: almost nothing, because you expected it.

steps.prompt: An event that is certain to happen carries 1 bit of information.
steps.explanation: False. With $p$ = 1, $I = -\log_2 1$ = **0 bits**: you learn nothing from being told what you already knew. 1 bit is the information of an event with $p$ = 1/2.

steps.title: Bits and nats
steps.body: The base of the logarithm only sets the unit: $\log_2$ gives bits, $\ln$ gives nats, $\log_{10}$ gives hartleys. 1 nat is $1/\ln 2$ = 1.443 bits.

steps.prompt: An outcome carries {{x}} nats of information.

ask.prompt: What was the probability of the outcome?
ask.explanation: In nats $I = -\ln p$, so $p = e^{-I} = e^{-{{x}}}$ = **{{exp(-x)}}**. (Check in bits: $2^{-{{x/ln(2)}}}$ gives the same.)

steps.title: Average surprise
steps.body: Average the information over all outcomes, weighted by how often each one occurs: that is the **entropy** $H(X)$ in bits per symbol. A source that nearly always sends the same symbol has a low entropy, even though its rare symbol is very informative when it does appear.

steps.prompt: A source emits A, B and C with probabilities {{a}}, {{b}} and {{c}}. What is its entropy?
steps.explanation: $H = -\sum p_i\log_2 p_i$ = {{a}} × {{-log2(a)}} + {{b}} × {{-log2(b)}} + {{c}} × {{-log2(c)}} = **{{-a*log2(a) - b*log2(b) - c*log2(c)}} bits/symbol** (each term is probability × information). The maximum for 3 symbols would be $\log_2 3$ = 1.585 bits.

steps.prompt: Each source below has four symbols with the probabilities shown. Which one has the **highest** entropy?
steps.explanation: Equal probabilities give the maximum, $\log_2 4$ = **2 bits**. The others: (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1) gives 1.85 bits, (0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1) gives 1.36 bits, and (0.5, 0.5, 0, 0) is really a 2-symbol source with 1 bit.

steps.title: The binary entropy function
steps.body: For a binary source with $P(1) = p$ the entropy is a function of $p$ alone, written $H(p)$. It is 0 at $p$ = 0 and $p$ = 1 and peaks at 1 bit for $p$ = 0.5. Drag $p$.

steps.prompt: A binary source sends a 1 with probability {{p}}. What is its entropy?
Drag $p$ (at most 0.5) until the binary source has an entropy of {{h}} bit.
steps.explanation: $H(p)$ = {{h}} bit for $p$ ≈ **{{pt||2}}** (and, by symmetry, for 1 − {{pt||2}} = {{1-pt||2}}). Check: {{pt||3}} × {{-log2(pt)||3}} + {{1-pt||3}} × {{-log2(1-pt)||3}} ≈ {{h}}. Note how far from 0.5 you must go: the curve is flat near its peak.

steps.prompt: A source with {{M}} symbols can have an entropy of {{log2(M) + d}} bits/symbol.
steps.explanation: The entropy of {{M}} symbols can be anything from 0 up to $\log_2 {{M}}$ = {{log2(M)}} bits (all symbols equally likely), but never more. So {{log2(M)+d}} bits/symbol is possible exactly when it does not exceed {{log2(M)}} bits.

steps.title: Maximum entropy
steps.body: With $M$ symbols the entropy is largest when all symbols are equally likely: then every symbol is equally surprising and nothing can be predicted. The maximum is $\log_2 M$. Any bias lowers it, down to 0 for a source that always sends the same symbol.

steps.prompt: A keypad sends one of {{M}} keys. What is the largest possible entropy per key press?
steps.explanation: The maximum is reached when all {{M}} keys are equally likely: $H_{max} = \log_2 {{M}}$ = **{{log2(M)}} bits**. Note that this need not be a whole number of bits.

steps.prompt: A source emits A, B, C and D with probabilities {{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}} and {{d}}. What is its entropy?
steps.explanation: $H$ = {{a}} × {{-log2(a)}} + {{b}} × {{-log2(b)}} + {{c}} × {{-log2(c)}} + {{d}} × {{-log2(d)}} = **{{-a*log2(a) - b*log2(b) - c*log2(c) - d*log2(d)}} bits/symbol** (maximum for 4 symbols: 2 bits).

steps.prompt: A weather station sends one of three states per reading: sunny ({{a}}), cloudy ({{b}}) or rain ({{c}}), at {{rs}} readings per second.

ask.prompt: What is the entropy per reading?

ask.explanation: $H$ = {{Hs}} bits per reading, so $R = r_s H$ = {{rs}} × {{Hs}} = **{{rs*Hs|bit/s}}**.

steps.prompt: A binary sensor outputs a 1 with probability {{p}}. Its readings are stored with 1 bit each. What fraction of the stored bits is redundant, $1 - H/1\ \text{bit}$?
steps.explanation: $H({{p}})$ = {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} bit, so a fraction 1 − {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} = **{{1 - (-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}}** of the stored bits carries no information. A good compressor could remove it.

steps.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Compare the information in the ordered pair (first, second) with the information in only their sum.
steps.explanation: The pair has 36 equally likely outcomes: $\log_2 36$ = **5.17 bits**. The sum takes 11 values with probabilities 1/36, 2/36, …, 6/36, …, 1/36, so $H = -\sum p\log_2 p$ = **3.27 bits**, less than $\log_2 11$ = 3.46 bits because the sums are not equally likely. 2.58 bits is the information of one die only. Throwing away which die showed what loses information.

steps.prompt: Match each source (its symbol probabilities) to its entropy.
steps.explanation: With powers of 1/2 every term is easy: $-\log_2$ of 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 is 1, 2, 3 bits. E.g. (1/2, 1/4, 1/4): 0.5·1 + 0.25·2 + 0.25·2 = 1.5 bits. A certain outcome gives 0 bits.

steps.prompt: A binary source sends a 1 with probability {{p}}. What is its entropy in **nats**?
steps.explanation: In bits, $H$ = {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}}. One bit is $\ln 2$ = 0.693 nat, so $H$ = {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} × 0.693 = **{{((-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p)))*ln(2)}} nats**. (Or directly with $\ln$: $-p\ln p - (1-p)\ln(1-p)$.)

steps.prompt: A link carries {{Rb|bit/s}}. With ideal compression, how many readings per second of a binary sensor with $P(1)$ = {{p}} can it carry?
steps.explanation: Ideal compression needs $H({{p}})$ = {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} bit per reading on average (instead of 1 bit). Readings per second = {{Rb|bit/s}} / {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} bit = **{{Rb/(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))||3}}**.

steps.prompt: Doubling the number of equally likely symbols adds exactly 1 bit to the entropy.
steps.explanation: True. $\log_2(2M) = \log_2 M + 1$: one extra yes/no question (which half?) is needed.

steps.title: How much information is in English?
steps.body: A uniform model of 26 letters plus space gives $\log_2 27$ = 4.75 bits per character. Single-letter frequencies lower this to about 4.1 bits. Context helps far more: after 'informatio' the next letter is almost certainly 'n'. Prediction experiments put English at roughly 1 to 1.5 bits per letter, which is why text compresses so well.

steps.prompt: A compressor stores English text at {{b}} bits per character. The original file uses 8-bit ASCII. What compression ratio (original size / compressed size) does it reach?
steps.explanation: Ratio = 8 bits / {{b}} bits = **{{8/b}}**. Better models of the language (longer context) push $b$ further towards the 1 to 1.5 bits/letter that English really contains.

steps.prompt: A temperature sensor is read by a 12-bit ADC. Between consecutive samples the code changes by −1, 0 or +1 with probabilities {{q}}, {{1-2*q}} and {{q}} (larger steps never occur).

ask.prompt: What is the entropy of the differences?
By what factor could ideal coding of the differences shrink the data, compared with sending every 12-bit sample?
ask.explanation: The differences carry only $H$ = {{Hd}} bits per sample (the first sample is sent once in full). Factor = 12 / {{Hd}} = **{{12/Hd}}**.

steps.prompt: {{n}} fair coins are tossed, and you are told only **how many** came up heads. How much information does that give on average?
steps.explanation: The number of heads $k$ is binomial: $P(k) = \binom{ {{n}} }{k}/2^{ {{n}} }$. Then $H = -\sum_k P(k)\log_2 P(k)$ = **{{-sum(k, 0, n, choose(n, k)/2^n*log2(choose(n, k)/2^n))}} bits**, much less than the {{n}} bits of the full sequence: the count does not say **which** coins were heads.

steps.prompt: A coin with $P(\text{heads})$ = {{p}} is flipped until the first head appears. What is the entropy of the number of flips $X$?
steps.hint: Average $-\log_2 P(X = k)$ with $P(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p$ and $E[X] = 1/p$; the result simplifies to $H(p)/p$.
steps.explanation: $X$ is geometric: $P(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p$. Averaging $-\log_2 P(X)$ gives $-\log_2 p - (E[X] - 1)\log_2(1-p)$ with $E[X] = 1/p$, which simplifies to $H(p)/p$. Here $H({{p}})$ = {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} bit, so $H(X)$ = {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} / {{p}} = **{{((-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p)))/p}} bits**. Although $X$ has infinitely many values, its entropy is finite.

steps.prompt: A binary source with $P(1)$ = {{p}} produces a block of {{n}} independent bits. What is the entropy of the whole block?
steps.explanation: For independent symbols the entropies add: $H = nH(p)$ = {{n}} × {{(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} = **{{n*(-p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p))}} bits**, against {{n}} bits for a uniform source. Almost all of the probability sits on roughly $2^{nH(p)}$ 'typical' blocks, a tiny fraction of the $2^{ {{n}} }$ possible ones; that is why such data compress to about $nH(p)$ bits.

steps.prompt: Which statement about entropy is correct?
options: It depends only on the probabilities, not on the symbol values
Relabelling the symbols with larger numbers increases it
It is always a whole number of bits
A source with more symbols always has a higher entropy
steps.explanation: $H = -\sum p_i\log_2 p_i$ uses only the probabilities: renaming symbols changes nothing. It is rarely a whole number (e.g. 1.585 bits for 3 equally likely symbols), and a 100-symbol source that almost always sends one symbol has a lower entropy than a fair coin.

steps.prompt: Storing English text as 8-bit ASCII is redundant even under the crudest model, a uniform choice among 27 characters.
steps.explanation: True. A uniform model needs only $\log_2 27$ = 4.75 bits per character, so at least 8 − 4.75 = 3.25 of every 8 bits are redundant, and real English (about 1 to 1.5 bits/letter) is far more redundant still.
